items.author: Sahara Vacation Team
items.title: Erg Chigaga vs Erg Chebbi: Which Moroccan Sahara Dunes Should You Choose?
items.content: Erg Chebbi and Erg Chigaga are Morocco's two great Saharan dune fields. This guide compares distance, access, crowds, trekking and price so you can pick the right desert tour for your trip.

body.text: Most travelers planning a Morocco desert tour end up weighing the same two names: Erg Chebbi, the famous golden wall of sand behind Merzouga, and Erg Chigaga, the wild, much quieter dune field that waits almost an hour of off-road track past M'Hamid El Ghizlane. Both are true Sahara, both end with a night under an absurd number of stars, and both will ruin ordinary beaches for you. But they deliver completely different experiences.

The short answer: choose Erg Chebbi if it is your first Sahara trip, your time is short, or you want an easy-to-reach classic dune sunset with the widest choice of camps. Choose Erg Chigaga if you want real remoteness, long camel treks, and a dune field you may have to yourself. You truly cannot go wrong — but you should pick on purpose, not by accident.
Erg Chebbi at a glance

items: Where: about 25 km from Erfoud, behind the village of Merzouga, near the Algerian border.
Size: a compact ridge roughly 22 km long, with crests rising about 150 metres.
Access: asphalt almost to the dunes — the easiest real Sahara in Morocco to reach.
Vibe: lively, well-serviced, endlessly photographed. Camps range from simple tents to luxury glamping with private bathrooms.
Good for: first-timers, families, short itineraries, and everyone on a Marrakech–Fès loop who wants the classic camel-at-sunset shot.

body.text: Erg Chigaga at a glance

items: Where: about 55 km of desert track past M'Hamid El Ghizlane, in the Draa valley region.
Size: a far bigger, lower-slung field of dunes — some crests climb well over double the height of Chebbi's.
Access: partly unpaved; the last stretch is 4x4 country. That remoteness is the whole point.
Vibe: silence, space, handfuls of camps. Fires, music, and no queue for the sunset viewpoint.
Good for: adventurous travelers, photographers, and anyone who bragged about getting off the beaten path.

body.text: Distance and access
From Marrakech, both dune fields are roughly a full day's drive (8–10 hours) — so the transfer day ends up being a highlight, not lost time.

To Erg Chebbi the road is tarmac the whole way, passing the Atlas mountains, Aït Ben Haddou, the Dades Gorges and the Todra Gorge — a scenic loop that fits perfectly into a [4-day Marrakech-to-Merzouga desert tour](/tours/atlas-au-sahara).

To Erg Chigaga you cross the Draa valley palm groves to Zagora, then drop south to M'Hamid, where the road ends. From there, a 4x4 carries you across stony desert to the dune field, passing nomad camps and the odd wild camel along the way.
The practical difference is simple: Chebbi is a day trip from Merzouga village; Chigaga is an expedition to the edge of the empty quarter.
Crowds and atmosphere

Erg Chebbi is Morocco's most-visited dune field — and for good reason: it is spectacular and easy. In October–April you will share the sunset ridge with other travelers. Merzouga has grown into a proper desert town with convenience stores, bike rentals, and dozens of camps.

Erg Chigaga is the opposite: even in high season, the dune field has very few camps and the silence is the headline. Sunrise typically means a wake-up call of hot tea and a companion who drives off after finding you a private dune. For couples and solo travelers chasing actual solitude, this is the clear winner.
Camel treks, activities and nights

items: Erg Chebbi: classic 1- to 2-hour camel treks to camp at sunset, sandboarding, quad bikes, Jeep tours — and an easy next-day sunrise before heading back to the road.

Erg Chigaga: longer, deeper treks — 2, 3, or more days of riding or walking across the dunes with a guide, camping each night in a wilder spot than the last. Sandboarding works even better on the taller, steeper slopes.

body.text: Both fields offer [stargazing camps](/tours/camp-nuit-etoiles), and both deserve a night or two — one night barely scratches the surface.
Price and tours

Erg Chebbi tours are cheaper on average, thanks to shared departures and competition. A [4-day Atlas-to-Sahara tour](/tours/atlas-au-sahara) or our [8-day grand Sahara loop](/tours/grande-traversee-sahara) both spend a full day and nights at the dunes.

Erg Chigaga tours cost a little more because of the 4x4 transfers and remoteness — real value for your privacy. Try the [M'Hamid–Erg Chigaga 3-day trek](/tours/circuit-3-jours-mhamid-erg-chigaga), or depart directly from [Marrakech](/tours/circuit-4-jours-marrakech-erg-chigaga), [Ouarzazate](/tours/circuit-3-jours-ouarzazate-erg-chigaga), or [Agadir](/tours/circuit-5-jours-agadir-erg-chegaga) on 4- and 5-day desert tours that finish on the Chigaga dunes.
Which should you pick?

items: Pick Erg Chebbi if: first trip · 2–4 days only in the desert · traveling with kids · you want the most comfortable camps · you're combining the desert with the Atlas/Todra loop.
Pick Erg Chigaga if: you've done the touristy stuff in Morocco · you want real remoteness · long camel trekking appeals · queues and crowds kill the magic for you.
Mix them: add a [stargazing camp](/tours/camp-nuit-etoiles) at Chebbi or Chigaga for an extra unforgettable night — the sky over both is genuinely among the darkest you can sleep under.

body.text: Can you visit both in one trip?

Technically yes, but we would advise against it: the two dune fields sit about 450 km apart by road, and rushing from one to the other turns a dream trip into a transport exercise. Pick one and do it properly — you will carry the memory a lot longer than the itinerary.
Frequently asked questions

items.q: Which dunes are taller — Erg Chebbi or Erg Chigaga?
items.a: Erg Chigaga has the higher crests — individually less iconic, but collectively it climbs more. Erg Chebbi's dunes are famously photogenic but more compact.

items.q: Which is closer to Marrakech?
items.a: The driving times are similar (8–10 hours), but Erg Chebbi is reachable entirely on asphalt, while Erg Chigaga needs an off-road 4x4 segment.

items.q: Are Erg Chebbi and Erg Chigaga both in the Sahara?
items.a: Yes. Both are true Saharan ergs (sand seas) in southeast Morocco, near the Algerian border — remote by European standards, routine for our team.

items.q: Which dune field is less touristy?
items.a: Erg Chigaga, without question. Its remoteness filters out the day-trippers, and its few camps rarely fill up.

items.q: What is the best time to visit the Moroccan desert?
items.a: October to April. The shoulder months (March and October) are the sweet spot — warm days, cool evenings, and clear skies for stargazing.

items.title: How Many Days Do You Need for a Morocco Desert Tour?
items.excerpt: Two, three, four or a week? The right length for a Sahara desert tour depends on where you start and what you want from the dunes. Honest advice with real drive times.
items.content: How many days you need for a Morocco desert tour depends on your starting city and the dunes you want to reach. From Marrakech, budget at least three days to sleep on the Erg Chigaga dunes near M'Hamid; two days works from closer gateways such as Ouarzazate, and a week unlocks the deep desert.
items.author: Sahara Vacation Team

body.text: How many days do you need for a Morocco desert tour? It is one of the first questions every traveler asks, and the honest answer is: it depends on where you start and which dunes you want to reach. The good news is that the Moroccan Sahara is easy to reach from several gateway cities, so there is a trip length that fits almost any schedule.
Start with the real distances

items: Marrakech to M'Hamid (gate to Erg Chigaga): about 520 km, roughly 9–10 hours of driving.
Marrakech to Zagora: about 350 km, roughly 6–7 hours.
Marrakech to Erg Chebbi (Merzouga): about 560 km, roughly 9–10 hours.
Ouarzazate to M'Hamid: about 3 hours — the closest real gateway to the Chigaga dunes.
Agadir to Erg Chigaga: roughly a day's drive through the Souss and the Anti-Atlas.

body.text: The desert simply is not a day trip from Marrakech. Plan at least one full overnight — and honestly two nights if you want the dune experience, not just a photo stop. Everything below assumes you start from one of these cities.
Two days: a taster that works from the right city

A two-day desert tour is genuinely worthwhile if you start in Ouarzazate (the shortest route to M'Hamid) or with the closer Zagora option from Marrakech. You get a camel trek at sunset, a night in camp under the stars, and sunrise over the sand before heading back. It is a compact taste — perfect for travelers who only have a weekend — but it leaves you wanting more.

From Ouarzazate, our [2-day Erg Chigaga circuit](/tours/circuit-2-jours-ouarzazate-erg-chigaga) is the classic choice. From M'Hamid itself, the [2-day camel trek](/tours/trek-sahara-marocain-2-jours) packs a full desert day into a tight window.
Three days: the sweet spot for most travelers

Three days is the length most people booking from Marrakech should plan for. You cross the Atlas and the Draa valley on day one, sleep in the desert on night one, enjoy a full day of dunes and camel trekking, and still have a relaxed return. It is enough time to feel the silence — not just see it.

items: [3-day camel trek from M'Hamid](/tours/trek-sahara-marocain-3-jours) — the classic multi-day trek option.
[3-day 4x4 circuit from M'Hamid to Erg Chigaga](/tours/circuit-3-jours-mhamid-erg-chigaga) — dunes, regs and hamadas beyond the paved roads.
[3-day circuit from Ouarzazate](/tours/circuit-3-jours-ouarzazate-erg-chigaga) — shorter transfers, more time on the sand.

body.text: Four to five days: space to breathe

With four or five days the pace softens completely. You can linger in the Drâa valley, add a second or third night in the desert, and take longer camel treks through the heart of the dunes. This is the length most travelers wish they had booked.

items: [4-day Marrakech to Erg Chigaga circuit](/tours/circuit-4-jours-marrakech-erg-chigaga) — Atlas, Aït Ben Haddou, the Drâa valley and two desert nights.
[5-day circuit from Agadir](/tours/circuit-5-jours-agadir-erg-chegaga) — the Souss, the Anti-Atlas and the Chigaga dunes.
[4-day and 5-day camel treks from M'Hamid](/tours/trek-sahara-marocain-4-jours) — true nomad-paced trekking.

body.text: A week or more: the deep desert

If you can spare a full week or more, the Moroccan Sahara reveals its real scale. Multi-day camel treks cross dune fields, dry riverbeds, oases and hamadas that almost nobody reaches, with camp moving each night alongside a caravan. This is the experience the desert was always meant to give.

Our [7-day trekking expedition](/tours/trek-sahara-marocain-7-jours), the [8-day grand trek](/tours/trek-sahara-marocain-8-jours), or the [Nomad & Berber immersion](/tours/immersion-nomade-berbere) are the deep-desert options, all departing from M'Hamid with transfers from Marrakech included.
The practical rule of thumb

items: 2 days: from Ouarzazate or as a Marrakech–Zagora taster.
3 days: the recommended minimum from Marrakech to the Chigaga dunes.
4–5 days: the comfort zone — more desert, more calm.
7 days or more: the full Sahara, at nomad pace.

body.text: Frequently asked questions

items.q: Can you do a desert tour from Marrakech in 2 days?
items.a: Yes, but only to the closer Zagora region. The big dunes of Erg Chigaga sit about 9–10 hours from Marrakech, so reaching them properly needs at least 3 days. For a genuine 2-day option, start from Ouarzazate.

items.q: How many days is best for a first Morocco desert tour?
items.a: Three days is the sweet spot for a first visit from Marrakech — one day to drive south, a full night and day on the dunes, and a relaxed return.

items.q: How far is Marrakech from the Sahara dunes?
items.a: About 520 km to M'Hamid (Erg Chigaga) and about 560 km to Merzouga (Erg Chebbi) — roughly 9–10 hours of driving each way.

items.q: Is a 2-day or 3-day desert tour better?
items.a: If you can spare the day, 3 days is clearly better: you reach bigger dunes, spend a full day in the desert, and the pace stops feeling rushed.

items.q: Which city is the best start for a short desert trip?
items.a: Ouarzazate is the closest gateway to M'Hamid and Erg Chigaga, making it ideal for 2- and 3-day circuits.

items.title: What to Pack for the Sahara Desert: A Camel Trek Packing List That Works
items.excerpt: Hot days, cold nights, blowing sand and a camel saddle. Here is the packing list that actually works for a Morocco desert trek — what to wear, what to leave at home.
items.content: Packing for the Sahara means dressing for two climates in one day. Light linen layers by day, a real warm layer for the night, closed shoes, a scarf and a small soft bag for the camel. Here is the full packing list.
items.author: Sahara Vacation Team

body.text: What to pack for the Sahara desert is the question we hear more than any other before a [camel trek](/tours/trek-sahara-marocain-3-jours). The desert looks simple — sand, sky, a night under the stars — but it asks a lot of your luggage. The golden rule is that you are dressing for two climates in one 24-hour cycle: hot and bright by day, genuinely cold after sunset.
Understand the temperature swing

In the desert around M'Hamid and Erg Chigaga, daytime highs reach 25–35°C in spring and autumn, and over 40°C in summer. But as soon as the sun drops, the sand radiates its heat away and nights fall fast: 20–25°C in summer nights, and 0–5°C in December and January. The swing between 4 pm and 4 am regularly exceeds 20°C. Pack for the night first — it is the part most travelers get wrong.
What to wear during the day

items: Lightweight long-sleeved shirt in linen or cotton — it blocks the sun better than a t-shirt and keeps you cooler.
Loose long trousers — fine cloth, not denim; comfortable on a camel saddle and respectful in the villages.
A large lightweight scarf (a tagelmust wrap) — sun, wind and sand protection in one, the desert's most useful item.
Wide-brim hat or cap and UV400 sunglasses — the glare off pale sand is far stronger than it looks.
Light neutral colours — white, beige, light blue reflect heat; black genuinely feels hotter.

body.text: What to pack for the night

items: A warm mid-layer — fleece or light down jacket. Non-negotiable all year; a real jacket in winter.
Warm socks and a beanie for winter nights on the dunes.
A thermal base layer (top and bottom) for December–February.
Comfortable sleepwear — the best camps provide blankets and bedding.

body.text: Footwear

items: Closed, comfortable shoes or light trail shoes for the camel ride and dune walking. Skip heavy hiking boots — they are hard work in soft sand.
A pair of sandals or flip-flops for relaxing at camp.
Socks you do not mind filling with sand.

body.text: The small things that make the difference

items: SPF 50+ sunscreen and lip balm with SPF — the sun works all year, and the dry air cracks lips fast.
A small power bank and a headlamp or small flashlight.
A reusable water bottle — you will drink more than you expect.
A ziplock or dust bag for camera and phone.
Personal medicines, wet wipes and tissues.

body.text: What to leave at home

items: Heavy hard-shell suitcases — take a small soft bag or backpack on the camel; your main luggage stays in the vehicle or hotel.
Denim and tight synthetic sportswear — uncomfortable on a saddle and in the heat.
Fancy shoes or high heels — they will not survive the sand.
More than one 'nice' outfit — everyone ends up wearing layers and a scarf.

body.text: One small bag for the camel

On a camel trek you ride with your overnight essentials and the rest stays behind. Pack a small soft backpack with your warm layer, water, camera, toiletries and medication. The caravan carries the camp, the cooking gear and the blankets — you just bring what you need.
Frequently asked questions

items.q: How cold does the Sahara get at night?
items.a: In December and January nights can drop to 0–5°C around M'Hamid and Erg Chigaga. Even in spring and autumn you will want a fleece or light jacket after sunset.

items.q: Can I wear shorts on a camel trek?
items.a: It is not recommended. Long, loose trousers protect your legs from the sun, the sand and the rough saddle blanket — they are cooler and more comfortable in practice.

items.q: Do desert camps provide blankets and heating?
items.a: Good camps provide multiple blankets, and some have a stove or heater in the communal tent. Ask your operator if the sleeping tent is heated when you book for winter.

items.q: What bag should I take on a camel trek?
items.a: A small, soft backpack with only your overnight essentials. Camels cannot easily carry hard suitcases.

items.q: Do I need sunscreen in winter?
items.a: Yes. The sun is lower but the reflection off pale sand still burns quickly, and the air is dry.

items.title: Best Time to Visit the Sahara Desert in Morocco (Month by Month)
items.excerpt: October to April is the sweet spot, but each month has its own character. Weigh weather, crowds and prices month by month to pick the season that fits your trip.
items.content: The best time to visit the Sahara desert in Morocco is October to April. October, November, March and April offer the most comfortable temperatures; winter brings the clearest skies and fewest crowds; summer is only for the heat-tolerant.
items.author: Sahara Vacation Team

body.text: Best time to visit the Sahara desert in Morocco? The short answer for most travelers is October to April. But within that window each month has its own personality — and the right choice depends on whether you want perfect light for photography, the fewest crowds, or the lowest prices. Here is the honest month-by-month picture from our team, who live at the edge of the dunes.
October to April: the reliable sweet spot

Through these months, daytime temperatures around M'Hamid and Erg Chigaga sit comfortably between 20°C and 30°C — warm enough for camel trekking, cool enough for long walks on the dunes. Nights are crisp rather than punishing, and the skies stay clear for stargazing. This is the window in which most of our [desert treks](/tours/trek-sahara-marocain-3-jours) run.
October and November: the autumn sweet spot

Autumn is many guides' favourite season. The summer heat has gone, the light turns low and golden, and the sandstorm risk is close to zero. November is quiet while still beautiful — fewer camps, earlier sunsets, and some of the richest golden hours of the year for photography.
December to February: cold nights, empty dunes

Winter days are genuinely pleasant — 18 to 22°C, perfect for walking — but nights can drop to 0–5°C, so warm layers are essential. The reward is the quietest, clearest desert of the year: fewer travelers, cleaner air, and the best stargazing in Morocco. December–January is the calmest booking window apart from the Christmas rush.
March and April: spring light and warm days

Spring brings warm days (up to 30°C by afternoon), wonderful light, and after rare rains, brief wildflowers across the desert floor. The trade-off is wind: the Chergui sandstorm season runs mainly from late March through May, though storms usually pass within hours. Book camps early — this is the busiest window of the year.
May and September: the transition months

Both months are workable if you keep to the cool hours. May is hot by the afternoon and windier; September is still warm but easing. Mornings and evenings remain beautiful — perfect for a sunrise camel trek and early departure.
June to August: only for heat lovers

Summer in the deep south is extreme: daytime highs frequently exceed 40°C and can push past 45°C. Treks are limited to sunrise and sunset hours, and the desert is genuinely empty. Prices are at their lowest, but unless you are truly heat-tolerant, October to April is the wiser choice.
The monthly quick reference

items: January–February: clear, quiet, cold nights. Best for stargazers who pack warm (low–medium crowds).
March–April: warm, photogenic, busier. Watch for spring sandstorms (high crowds).
May: early-season heat build-up; morning treks (medium).
June–August: extreme heat; empty dunes; lowest prices (very low).
September: warm but easing; a good late-season window (medium).
October–November: the autumn sweet spot — ideal light, calm air (high for good reason).
December: mild days, cold nights, Christmas rush, then quiet (high at the holidays).

body.text: Frequently asked questions

items.q: What is the single best month to visit the Sahara in Morocco?
items.a: Many guides would say October: warm days, cool nights, low wind, golden light and manageable crowds. November, March and April are nearly as good.

items.q: Is summer a bad time to visit the desert?
items.a: It is the most challenging season — regular 40°C+ days — but doable if you trek at sunrise and sunset and rest through the middle of the day.

items.q: Is winter too cold for a desert night?
items.a: No, it is one of the most rewarding seasons. Nights can touch 0°C, so you pack proper layers — in return you get the clearest skies and the quietest dunes all year.

items.q: What are the best months for camel trekking?
items.a: October, November, March and April offer the most comfortable conditions for treks such as our [multi-day expeditions](/tours/trek-sahara-marocain-7-jours).

items.q: When is the sandstorm season?
items.a: Mainly late March through May (the Chergui wind), with occasional dust days in October. Storms usually pass within a few hours.

body.text: Whatever the month, the desert delivers — the difference is in the details. To compare treks and dates, browse our [camel treks](/tours/trek-sahara-marocain-7-jours) or [message us on WhatsApp](https://wa.me/212674283639) with your dates.
